title: Time, Frequency, Degree, Manner, and Place Adverbs
goal: Use common Norwegian adverbs and place them correctly in simple main clauses.

objectives.statement: Use common Norwegian adverbs and place them correctly in simple main clauses.

spans.value: Maja and Erik are meeting at a café before a volunteer-group meeting. Maja wants to practise what she will say.
Kommer du ofte hit så tidlig?

blocks.translation: Do you often come here this early?

spans.value: Ja, jeg jobber vanligvis hjemme, men i dag møter jeg deg her.

blocks.translation: Yes, I usually work at home, but today I’m meeting you here.

spans.value: Bra. Jeg snakker alltid ganske fort på møter.

blocks.translation: Good. I always speak quite fast in meetings.

spans.value: I dag snakker vi rolig sammen her først.

blocks.translation: Today we’ll speak calmly together here first.

spans.value: Fint. Jeg skriver notatene veldig tydelig.

blocks.translation: Good. I write the notes very clearly.

spans.value: Prosjektlederen kommer snart. Hun sykler vanligvis hit, og hun sykler veldig fort.

blocks.translation: The project leader is coming soon. She usually cycles here, and she cycles very fast.

spans.value: Da finner vi et bord inne nå.

blocks.translation: Then we’ll find a table inside now.

spans.value: The conversation gives us more than information about a meeting. The adverbs tell us when things happen, how often they happen, how they happen, where they happen, and to what degree something is true.

en.value: The project leader is coming soon.

spans.value: Each adverb adds a particular kind of meaning. Correct position helps the listener connect that meaning to the right part of the sentence.
can describe a verb, an adjective, another adverb, or the situation expressed by a whole clause. In this chapter, we will work with five useful kinds of information:

items.value: Degree tells us how strong or complete something is:
Manner tells us how an action happens:
Place tells us where or in which direction:

spans.value: You do not need to label every adverb before speaking. The practical question is simpler: what detail are you adding, and where does that detail normally go?
In a neutral main clause beginning with the subject, common frequency adverbs usually come after the finite verb—the verb carrying tense.
subject + finite verb + frequency adverb + remaining information
, with the frequency adverb before the main verb. Norwegian normally places it after the finite verb:
With a verb phrase containing an auxiliary or modal verb, the frequency adverb still follows the finite verb:

en.value: She has always worked at home.

spans.value: are finite. The adverb follows them rather than moving beside the final verb.

sections.title: Degree: keep it close to what it strengthens

spans.value: Degree adverbs usually stand directly before the adjective or adverb they modify.
The degree adverb and the word it modifies form a close unit:
This explains the order in Maja’s sentence:

no.value: Jeg snakker alltid ganske fort på møter.

en.value: I always speak quite fast in meetings.

spans.value: describes how often she speaks that way. It follows the finite verb
The sentence therefore builds in layers:

no.value: Jeg | snakker | alltid | ganske fort | på møter.

en.value: I | speak | always | quite fast | in meetings.

spans.value: Do not separate a degree adverb from the adjective or adverb it modifies:
should always go directly after the verb because it feels like an important adverb. Its position depends on what it modifies. In
, so the two words stay together.

sections.title: Manner: usually after the action or its object

spans.value: Manner adverbs describe how an action happens. When there is no object, manner commonly follows the verb:
When the verb has an object, the object normally comes before the manner adverb:
describes how she writes. It is an adverb and comes after the object. In the second sentence,
. That adjective pattern is not our focus here; the contrast simply shows why
With degree added, the whole manner expression stays together:

en.value: Maja writes the notes very clearly.
Erik reads the plan quite slowly.

sections.title: Place and time at the end

spans.value: Place and time information often appears toward the end of a neutral main clause.

en.value: The project leader is coming soon.

spans.value: When a sentence contains both place and time, place commonly comes before time:

no.value: Vi møtes på kafeen i dag.

en.value: We are meeting at the café today.
Erik works at home in the morning.

spans.value: When manner, place, and time all occur at the end, a useful neutral order is:

en.value: We are speaking calmly here now.

no.value: Hun sykler fort til kafeen hver morgen.

en.value: She cycles quickly to the café every morning.

no.value: Erik leser planen nøye hjemme om kvelden.

en.value: Erik reads the plan carefully at home in the evening.

spans.value: This is a strong default, not a claim that Norwegian sentences can never vary. Speakers may move information to highlight it. For clear A2 main clauses, however,
gives you a reliable neutral order.

no.value: Erik arbeider vanligvis rolig hjemme om morgenen.

en.value: Erik usually works calmly at home in the morning.

spans.value: The sentence follows a useful full pattern:
subject + finite verb + frequency + manner + place + time
If an object is present, it comes before the end information:

no.value: Erik leser ofte planen nøye hjemme om kvelden.

en.value: Erik often reads the plan carefully at home in the evening.

no.value: Erik | leser | ofte | planen | nøye | hjemme | om kvelden.

en.value: Erik | reads | often | the plan | carefully | at home | in the evening.

spans.value: Do not push the object behind a final time expression:

sections.title: Time or place first: the verb remains second

spans.value: Time and place expressions can also come first when the speaker wants to establish the setting.

no.value: Jeg møter Erik på kafeen i dag.

en.value: I’m meeting Erik at the café today.

no.value: I dag møter jeg Erik på kafeen.

en.value: Today I’m meeting Erik at the café.

spans.value: Both sentences are correct. The second makes
Norwegian main clauses follow the verb-second pattern: when time or place comes first, the finite verb comes next, before the subject.

en.value: In the morning he works at home.
At the café Maja often practises.

spans.value: The opening expression occupies the first position. The finite verb occupies the second:
Avoid keeping English subject–verb order after a fronted time expression:
The same frequency rule still operates later in the clause:

no.value: På kafeen øver Maja ofte om morgenen.

en.value: At the café Maja often practises in the morning.

spans.value: comes second, followed by the subject
The project leader, Nora, arrives at the café.
Hei! Jeg kommer vanligvis litt tidligere, men bussen kjørte veldig sakte i dag.

blocks.translation: Hi! I usually arrive a little earlier, but the bus went very slowly today.

spans.value: Det går bra. Maja øver rolig her nå.

blocks.translation: That’s fine. Maja is practising calmly here now.

spans.value: Ja, og jeg snakker ikke så fort i dag.

blocks.translation: Yes, and I’m not speaking so fast today.

spans.value: Flott. På møtet snakker du alltid tydelig.

blocks.translation: Great. At the meeting you always speak clearly.

spans.value: Nora’s first sentence contains several different details:

en.value: I usually arrive a little earlier.

no.value: Bussen kjørte veldig sakte i dag.

en.value: The bus went very slowly today.

spans.value: gives time and comes at the end.
Erik uses the full end pattern:

en.value: Maja is practising calmly here now.

no.value: På møtet snakker du alltid tydelig.

en.value: At the meeting you always speak clearly.

spans.value: follows the subject in this fronted structure.

no.value: Du snakker alltid tydelig på møtet.

en.value: You always speak clearly at the meeting.

no.value: På møtet snakker du alltid tydelig.

en.value: At the meeting you always speak clearly.

spans.value: The information is similar, but the second sentence makes the meeting the point of departure.

no.value: Maja skriver i dag notatene tydelig.

en.value: Maja writes today the notes clearly.

no.value: Maja skriver notatene tydelig i dag.

en.value: Maja writes the notes clearly today.

spans.value: comes before the manner and time information.
Forgetting verb-second order after a fronted expression

en.value: In the morning Erik works at home.
In the morning Erik works at home.

spans.value: must follow the opening time expression.
Adverbs do not all occupy one universal “adverb position.”

no.value: Hun sykler vanligvis veldig fort til jobb om morgenen.

en.value: She usually cycles very fast to work in the morning.

items.value: follows the finite verb because it gives frequency.

spans.value: Frequency follows the finite verb. Degree stays beside its target. Objects come before end details. Manner, place, and time usually form the end sequence. A fronted time or place expression is followed by the finite verb.
The next week, Maja is preparing at the library rather than at the café.

no.value: Maja arbeider ofte stille på biblioteket om ettermiddagen.

en.value: Maja often works quietly at the library in the afternoon.

no.value: Hun leser notatene veldig nøye der.

en.value: She reads the notes very carefully there.

no.value: I dag møter hun Nora på biblioteket.

en.value: Today she is meeting Nora at the library.

no.value: De snakker rolig sammen inne nå.

en.value: They are speaking calmly together inside now.

spans.value: In the library setting, build similar sentences without relying on wording from the café dialogue.

Without looking back, describe three facts about Maja’s preparation: one routine, one action with a degree-and-manner expression, and one action set in a particular place or time. Then rewrite the final sentence so that its time or place expression comes first.
